claim: The orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) is classically linked to inhibitory control, emotion regulation, and reward processing.
source: Orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) is classically linked to inhibitory control, emotion regulation, and reward processing.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research in the field.

claim: Recent perspectives propose that the OFC generates predictions about perceptual events, actions, and their outcomes.
source: Recent perspectives propose that the OFC also generates predictions about perceptual events, actions, and their outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent theoretical perspectives.

claim: OFC patients showed an attenuated mismatch negativity (MMN) to local prediction violation.
source: However, patients showed an attenuated mismatch negativity (MMN) and P3a to local prediction violation
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental ERP data comparing OFC patients to controls.

claim: OFC patients showed an attenuated P3a to local prediction violation.
source: However, patients showed an attenuated mismatch negativity (MMN) and P3a to local prediction violation
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental ERP data comparing OFC patients to controls.

claim: OFC patients showed a diminished MMN to combined local and global level prediction violation.
source: as well as a diminished MMN followed by a delayed P3a to the combined local and global level prediction violation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental ERP data comparing OFC patients to controls.

claim: OFC patients showed a delayed P3a to combined local and global level prediction violation.
source: as well as a diminished MMN followed by a delayed P3a to the combined local and global level prediction violation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental ERP data comparing OFC patients to controls.

claim: The P3b component to conditions involving violations of prediction at the level of global rules was preserved in the OFC group.
source: The subsequent P3b component to conditions involving violations of prediction at the level of global rules was preserved in the OFC group.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental ERP data showing no significant differences between OFC patients and controls.

claim: Comparable effects were absent in patients with lesions restricted to the lateral PFC.
source: Comparable effects were absent in patients with lesions restricted to the lateral PFC, which lends a degree of anatomical specificity to the altered predictive processing resulting from OFC lesion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental ERP data comparing LPFC patients to controls.

claim: The altered magnitudes and time courses of MMN/P3a responses after lesions to the OFC indicate that the neural correlates of detection of auditory regularity violation are impacted at two hierarchical levels of rule abstraction.
source: Overall, the altered magnitudes and time courses of MMN/P3a responses after lesions to the OFC indicate that the neural correlates of detection of auditory regularity violation are impacted at two hierarchical levels of rule abstraction.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental ERP data.

claim: The OFC is linked to goal-directed attention.
source: The orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) is linked to multiple high-level cognitive processes, including inhibitory control (Godefroy et al., 1999; Harlow, 1993; Picton et al., 2007), goal-directed attention (Badre and Wagner, 2004; Luu et al., 2000; Walton et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The OFC is linked to temporal context memory.
source: temporal context memory (Duarte et al., 2010; Shimamura et al., 1990)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The OFC is linked to working memory (WM) maintenance.
source: and working memory (WM) maintenance (Llorens et al., 2019; Barbey et al., 2011; D'Esposito et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The OFC plays a pivotal role in decision-making.
source: all supporting pivotal involvement of the OFC in decision-making (Bechara et al., 2000a; Ernst et al., 2002; Hebscher and Gilboa, 2016; Ullsperger and von Cramon, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The OFC plays a key role in outcome monitoring and evaluation.
source: Extensive research has highlighted a key role of the OFC in outcome monitoring and evaluation (e.g., Walton et al., 2004; Ullsperger and von Cramon, 2004; Wallis, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The OFC plays a key role in the signaling of reward value.
source: and the signaling of reward value (Howard and Kahnt, 2021; Schoenbaum et al., 2009; Schoenbaum et al., 2011; Wikenheiser and Schoenbaum, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Patients with OFC damage typically demonstrate difficulty in learning from previous errors.
source: Patients with OFC damage typically demonstrate difficulty in learning from previous errors, often combined with reduced sensitivity to future consequences (Bechara et al., 2000a; Bechara et al., 2000b; Floden et al., 2008; Stuss et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The OFC forms representations of the environment that extend beyond reward.
source: However, studies using tasks where outcomes do not have a clear emotional or motivational value support the idea that the OFC forms representations of the environment that extend beyond reward (Schoenbaum et al., 2011; McDannald et al., 2014; Stalnaker et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: OFC generates specific predictions about impending events, such as their identity and features.
source: A recent proposal is that OFC generates specific predictions about impending events, such as their identity and features, and uses relevant contextual and temporal attributes to allow continuous updating of rules (Schuck et al., 2016; Stalnaker et al., 2015; Wilson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent theoretical proposals.

claim: Animal and human studies have reported a role of the OFC in signaling prediction errors (PEs).
source: Notably, animal (Sul et al., 2010; Thorpe et al., 1983; Wallis and Rich, 2011) and human (Nobre et al., 1999; Schultz and Dickinson, 2000; Tobler et al., 2006) studies have reported a role of the OFC in signaling PEs
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior animal and human studies.

claim: The brain continually formulates predictions about sensory inputs and tests them against incoming sensory signals.
source: According to the predictive coding hypothesis, the brain continually formulates predictions about sensory inputs and tests them against incoming sensory signals, wherein the bottom-up information represents the interaction between the prediction and the actual sensory input (i.e., PE) (Clark, 2013; Friston, 2005; Mumford, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to predictive coding theory.

claim: Predictive coding computational models have implicated the prefrontal cortex (PFC) in higher-order predictions and PE processing.
source: Predictive coding computational models have implicated the prefrontal cortex (PFC) in higher-order predictions and PE processing (Chennu et al., 2016; Garrido et al., 2008; Garrido et al., 2009a; Phillips et al., 2015; Phillips et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to computational modeling studies.

claim: The dorsal part of medial PFC (dmPFC) is thought to be specialized for reporting error as a deviation from predicted events.
source: The dorsal part of medial PFC (dmPFC) is thought to be specialized for reporting error as a deviation from predicted events (Alexander and Brown, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The ventral part of medial PFC (vmPFC), that is, OFC, has been proposed to integrate perceptual input from cortical and subcortical areas, together with memories of previous stimuli, to determine the current task context.
source: The ventral part of medial PFC (vmPFC), that is, OFC, has been proposed to integrate perceptual input from cortical and subcortical areas, together with memories of previous stimuli, to determine the current task context (Wilson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The fronto-centrally distributed MMN is usually elicited by an infrequent tone that differs in its acoustic properties from a monotonous sequence of preceding frequent tones.
source: The fronto-centrally distributed MMN is usually elicited by an infrequent tone that differs in its acoustic properties (e.g., pitch, loudness) from a monotonous sequence of preceding frequent tones and persists in the absence of overt attention (Näätänen et al., 1978; Näätänen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on MMN.

claim: Within the predictive coding framework, the MMN is interpreted as an early PE signal arising from prediction violation due to a top-down predictive contribution.
source: Within the predictive coding framework, the MMN is interpreted as an early PE signal arising from prediction violation due to a top-down predictive contribution (Garrido et al., 2009a; Garrido et al., 2007; Parmentier et al., 2011; Winkler, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to predictive coding interpretations of MMN.

claim: MMN generators are found in the superior temporal planes bilaterally (i.e., primary auditory cortices and superior temporal gyri), in bilateral prefrontal cortices (i.e., inferior frontal gyri), as well as the inferior circular sulcus of the insula.
source: In agreement with a hierarchical model transmitting predictions in a top-down fashion to lower sensory areas are the findings of fMRI, scalp- and intracranial EEG studies showing MMN generators in the superior temporal planes bilaterally (i.e., primary auditory cortices and superior temporal gyri), in bilateral prefrontal cortices (i.e., inferior frontal gyri), as well as the inferior circular sulcus of the insula (Garrido et al., 2009a; Phillips et al., 2015; Phillips et al., 2016; Opitz et al., 2002; Doeller et al., 2003; Liebenthal et al., 2003; Molholm et al., 2005; Shalgi and Deouell, 2007; Deouell, 2007; Garrido et al., 2009c; Nourski et al., 2018; Blenkmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to fMRI and EEG studies.

claim: The P3 complex (P3a and P3b), sensitive to the detection of unpredictable auditory events, is elicited after the MMN.
source: The P3 complex (P3a and P3b), sensitive to the detection of unpredictable auditory events, is elicited after the MMN (Chennu et al., 2013; Doricchi et al., 2021; Wacongne et al., 2011; El Karoui et al., 2015; Kompus et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on P3 components.

claim: The P3a is evoked by infrequent or novel stimuli and is typically interpreted as reflecting an involuntary attentional reorienting process.
source: The earlier and more fronto-centrally distributed P3a is evoked by infrequent or novel stimuli (Polich, 2007) and is typically interpreted as reflecting an involuntary attentional reorienting process (Escera and Corral, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on P3a.

claim: The P3b, with a centro-posterior maximum, is associated with context updating in WM and allocation of attentional resources to stimulus evaluation.
source: The P3b, with a centro-posterior maximum, is associated with context updating in WM (Polich, 2007; Donchin and Coles, 1988; Chao et al., 1995) and allocation of attentional resources to stimulus evaluation, (Picton, 1992)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on P3b.

claim: P3b is dependent on conscious awareness.
source: and is dependent on conscious awareness (Sergent et al., 2005; Del Cul et al., 2007; Bekinschtein et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on P3b and consciousness.

claim: Early PFC lesion studies using simple oddball tasks showed diminished MMN elicited by deviant tones within sequences of standard tones.
source: Early PFC lesion studies using simple oddball tasks showed diminished MMN elicited by deviant tones within sequences of standard tones (Alho et al., 1994; Alain et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior lesion studies.

claim: PFC injury reduced the amplitude of the frontal P3a to unexpected novel auditory stimuli, whereas the parietally distributed P3b to detected deviants remained intact.
source: In the same vein, PFC injury reduced the amplitude of the frontal P3a to unexpected novel auditory stimuli, whereas the parietally distributed P3b to detected deviants remained intact (Knight, 1984; Knight and Scabini, 1998; Løvstad et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior lesion studies.

claim: Løvstad et al., 2012 reported attenuation of the P3a to unexpected novel environmental sounds after damage to either lateral PFC (LPFC) or OFC.
source: Løvstad et al., 2012 reported attenuation of the P3a to unexpected novel environmental sounds after damage to either lateral PFC (LPFC) or OFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific prior study.

claim: Solbakk et al., 2021 showed that the N2b-P3a complex elicited by unexpected auditory sensory outcomes of self-initiated actions in OFC patients did not differ as clearly from the response to expected outcomes as for the healthy controls.
source: Moreover, Solbakk et al., 2021 showed that the N2b-P3a complex elicited by unexpected auditory sensory outcomes of self-initiated actions in OFC patients did not differ as clearly from the response to expected outcomes as for the healthy controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific prior study.

claim: Scalp EEG recordings were obtained during an auditory local–global paradigm from a control group of healthy adults, a group of patients with lesions to the OFC, and a lesion control group of patients with lesions to the LPFC.
source: Scalp EEG recordings were obtained during an auditory local–global paradigm from a control group of healthy adults, a group of patients with lesions to the OFC (Figure 1) and a lesion control group of patients with lesions to the LPFC (Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and data collection.

claim: The experiment had regular and irregular blocks, where the most common sequence could be either regular (xxxxx) or irregular (xxxxy), building up global expectations.
source: The experiment had regular and irregular blocks, where the most common sequence could be either regular (xxxxx) or irregular (xxxxy), building up global expectations (i.e., predictions).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design.

claim: When the last tone in the sequence is different from the previous, it constitutes a local deviant.
source: When the last tone in the sequence is different from the previous, it constitutes a local deviant.
evidence: This claim defines a key experimental condition.

claim: On rare occasions, deviant sequences were introduced, violating the global rule.
source: On rare occasions, deviant sequences were introduced, violating the global rule.
evidence: This claim describes a key experimental manipulation.

claim: Participants were asked to detect global violations.
source: Participants were asked to detect these global violations, which might simultaneously conform or not the local rules.

source: In total, four key conditions were generated: control (predictable tones at both local and global levels), local deviant (local rule violations), global deviant (global rule violations), and local + global deviant (combined local and global rule violations).

claim: Behavioral data were collected through written reports of the number of rare sequences detected per task block.
source: Behavioral data were collected through written reports of the number of rare sequences detected per task block.

source: Participants performed the task properly with an average error rate of 9.54% (SD 8.97) for the healthy control participants, 10.55% (SD 6.18) for the OFC lesion group, and 6.37% (SD 5.79) for the LPFC lesion group.

claim: There was no statistically significant difference between the counts of rare tone sequences of the CTR group compared to the OFC group.
source: There was no statistically significant difference between the counts of rare tone sequences of the CTR group compared to the OFC group [F(1, 24) = 0.11, p=0.75]

claim: Both CTR and OFC groups showed condition differences corresponding to a negative cluster in the data at 67–128 ms (i.e., MMN) for the CTR group and at 73–131 ms for the OFC group in response to local-level unpredicted tones.
source: Both groups showed condition differences corresponding to a negative cluster in the data at 67–128 ms (i.e., MMN) for the CTR group [t(13) = –6633.65, p=0.012, 61/64 channels] and at 73–131 ms for the OFC group [t(11) = –3734.49, p=0.035, 41/64 channels].

claim: Both CTR and OFC groups showed a positive cluster at 143–313 ms (i.e., P3a) for the CTR group, which extended from 145 to 344 ms for the OFC group in response to local-level unpredicted tones.
source: This was followed by a positive cluster at 143–313 ms (i.e., P3a) for the CTR group [t(13) = 24808.43, p<0.001, 60/64 channels], which extended from 145 to 344 ms for the OFC group [t(11) = 21796.75, p<0.001, 58/64 channels].
evidence: This claim reports ERP data for the P3a component.

claim: Analysis of the response to local-level unpredicted tones revealed a reduced MMN for the OFC patients compared to the CTR participants in a time window from 73 to 110 ms.
source: Analysis of the response to local-level unpredicted tones (xy│xY trials) revealed a reduced MMN for the OFC patients compared to the CTR participants in a time window from 73 to 110 ms [positive cluster: t(25) = 1396.79, p=0.028, 39/64 channels].

claim: The groups did not differ significantly in the time range (i.e., 140–350 ms) of the P3a for local-level unpredicted tones.
source: However, the groups did not differ significantly in the time range (i.e., 140–350 ms) of the P3a (positive cluster: p=0.22, negative cluster: p=0.53).
evidence: This claim reports a lack of group difference in ERP data.

claim: Latency analysis for the MMN and P3a did not show statistically significant differences between the two groups for local-level unpredicted tones.
source: Latency analysis for the MMN and P3a did not show statistically significant differences between the two groups.
evidence: This claim reports a lack of group difference in latency data.

claim: Responses to the standard tones predicted at both levels (xx│xX trials) did not diverge significantly between the OFC and the CTR group.
source: Interestingly, responses to the standard tones predicted at both levels (xx│xX trials) did not diverge significantly between the OFC and the CTR group (positive cluster: p=0.79, negative cluster: p=0.51)
evidence: This claim reports a lack of group difference in ERP data for standard tones.

claim: Responses to the standard tones predicted at both levels (xx│xX trials) did not diverge significantly between the LPFC and the CTR group.

claim: Analysis of the local deviance response in the time ranges of the MMN (i.e., 50–150 ms) and P3a (i.e., 140–350 ms) for the LPFC lesion control group did not reveal statistically significant differences between the LPFC and the CTR group.
source: Analysis of the local deviance response in the time ranges of the MMN (i.e., 50–150 ms) and P3a (i.e., 140–350 ms) for the LPFC lesion control group did not reveal statistically significant differences between the LPFC and the CTR group (MMN, negative cluster: p=0.85; P3a, negative cluster: p=0.99) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: Results revealed a significant condition effect captured by a positive cluster at posterior electrodes, which lasted from 381 to 714 ms for the CTR group, and from 419 to 799 ms for the OFC group for global deviance.
source: Results revealed a significant condition effect captured by a positive cluster at posterior electrodes, which lasted from 381 to 714 ms for the CTR group [t(13) = 10521.05, p=0.009, 33/64 channels], and from 419 to 799 ms for the OFC group [t(11) = 13120.99, p=0.01, 51/64 channels].

claim: The response to global deviance was long-lasting with no well-defined peak and had the classical posterior maximum scalp topography and latency of the P3b.
source: This response was long-lasting with no well-defined peak and had the classical posterior maximum scalp topography and latency of the P3b (Figure 4A).

claim: No statistically significant differences between the two groups were found in the time window (i.e., 380–800 ms, based on CTR and OFC group condition contrasts) of the P3b for global deviance.
source: No statistically significant differences between the two groups were found in the time window (i.e., 380–800 ms, based on CTR and OFC group condition contrasts) of the P3b (positive cluster: p=0.61, no significant negative cluster was detected) (Figure 4B).

claim: Latency analysis for the P3b did not show statistically significant differences between the two groups for global deviance.

claim: Latency analysis showed that the MMN was not significantly delayed at midline electrodes for local + global deviance.
source: Latency analysis showed that the MMN was not significantly delayed at midline electrodes [only a trend-level effect at FCz: t(24) = 2.26, p=0.033; and Cz: t(24) = 1.78, p=0.088 electrodes, which did not survive the false discovery rate (FDR) correction].

source: Group-level statistics performed on the MMN, P3a, and P3b time windows did not show significant differences between LPFC patients and controls (MMN, positive cluster: p=0.74; P3a, positive cluster: p=0.52; P3b, positive cluster: p=0.46).
